claim: Evolutionary changes in the anatomy and physiology of the female reproductive system underlie the origins and diversification of pregnancy in Eutherian ('placental') mammals.
source: Evolutionary changes in the anatomy and physiology of the female reproductive system underlie the origins and diversification of pregnancy in Eutherian ('placental') mammals.
evidence: This is a foundational statement drawing on established evolutionary biology and comparative anatomy knowledge.

claim: Developmental and evolutionary history constrains normal physiological functions and biases the ways in which dysfunction contributes to reproductive trait diseases and adverse pregnancy outcomes.
source: This developmental and evolutionary history constrains normal physiological functions and biases the ways in which dysfunction contributes to reproductive trait diseases and adverse pregnancy outcomes.
evidence: This is a theoretical framework statement based on evolutionary medicine principles.

claim: Gene expression changes in the human endometrium during pregnancy are associated with the evolution of human-specific traits and pathologies of pregnancy.
source: Here, we show that gene expression changes in the human endometrium during pregnancy are associated with the evolution of human-specific traits and pathologies of pregnancy.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by the comparative transcriptomic analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hundreds of genes gained or lost endometrial expression in the human lineage.
source: We found that hundreds of genes gained or lost endometrial expression in the human lineage.
evidence: This is directly supported by the ancestral reconstruction analysis showing 923 genes gained and 771 genes lost.

claim: HTR2B may contribute to human-specific maternal–fetal communication systems.
source: Among these are genes that may contribute to human-specific maternal–fetal communication (HTR2B) and maternal–fetal immunotolerance (PDCD1LG2) systems, as well as vascular remodeling and deep placental invasion (CORIN).
evidence: This is based on the gene expression data, functional assays, and enrichment in serotonin signaling pathways.

claim: PDCD1LG2 may contribute to maternal–fetal immunotolerance systems.
source: Among these are genes that may contribute to human-specific maternal–fetal communication (HTR2B) and maternal–fetal immunotolerance (PDCD1LG2) systems, as well as vascular remodeling and deep placental invasion (CORIN).
evidence: This is based on gene expression data, known function of PD-L2 in immune regulation, and expression in decidual cells.

claim: CORIN may contribute to vascular remodeling and deep placental invasion.
source: Among these are genes that may contribute to human-specific maternal–fetal communication (HTR2B) and maternal–fetal immunotolerance (PDCD1LG2) systems, as well as vascular remodeling and deep placental invasion (CORIN).
evidence: This is based on gene expression data and previously published studies showing CORIN promotes spiral artery remodeling and trophoblast invasion.

claim: Evolution of the structures and functions of female reproductive system and extraembryonic fetal membranes underlie the evolution of pregnancy.
source: Evolution of the structures and functions of female reproductive system and extraembryonic fetal membranes, for example, underlie the evolution of pregnancy (Armstrong et al., 2017; Hou et al., 2009; Kin et al., 2015; Lynch et al., 2015; Lynch et al., 2008) and likely adverse pregnancy outcomes such as infertility (Cummins, 1999), recurrent spontaneous abortion (Kosova et al., 2015), preeclampsia (Carter, 2011; Crosley et al., 2013; Elliot, 2017; Rosenberg and Trevathan, 2007), and preterm birth (LaBella et al., 2020; Marinić et al., 2021; Plunkett et al., 2011; Swaggart et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Evolutionary changes in the female reproductive system likely contribute to adverse pregnancy outcomes such as infertility, recurrent spontaneous abortion, preeclampsia, and preterm birth.
source: Evolution of the structures and functions of female reproductive system and extraembryonic fetal membranes, for example, underlie the evolution of pregnancy (Armstrong et al., 2017; Hou et al., 2009; Kin et al., 2015; Lynch et al., 2015; Lynch et al., 2008) and likely adverse pregnancy outcomes such as infertility (Cummins, 1999), recurrent spontaneous abortion (Kosova et al., 2015), preeclampsia (Carter, 2011; Crosley et al., 2013; Elliot, 2017; Rosenberg and Trevathan, 2007), and preterm birth (LaBella et al., 2020; Marinić et al., 2021; Plunkett et al., 2011; Swaggart et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research on adverse pregnancy outcomes.

claim: Extant mammals span major stages in the evolution and diversification of pregnancy, including the origins of maternal provisioning (matrotrophy), placentation, and viviparity.
source: Extant mammals span major stages in the evolution and diversification of pregnancy, including the origins of maternal provisioning (matrotrophy), placentation, and viviparity (Behringer et al., 2006; Freyer et al., 2003; Freyer and Renfree, 2009; Hughes and Hall, 1998; Renfree, 1995; Renfree and Shaw, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research on mammalian reproduction.

claim: Eutherian mammals have evolved a complex suite of traits that support prolonged pregnancies such as an interrupted estrous cycle, maternal recognition of pregnancy, maternal–fetal communication, immunotolerance of the antigenically distinct fetus, and implantation of the blastocyst into maternal tissue.
source: Eutherian mammals have also evolved a complex suite of traits that support prolonged pregnancies such as an interrupted estrous cycle, maternal recognition of pregnancy, maternal–fetal communication, immunotolerance of the antigenically distinct fetus, and implantation of the blastocyst into maternal tissue (Abbot and Rokas, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Catarrhine primates have evolved spontaneous decidualization of endometrial stromal fibroblasts into decidual stromal cells under the combined action of progesterone, cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), and other unknown maternal signals.
source: Catarrhine primates, for example, have evolved spontaneous decidualization (differentiation) of endometrial stromal fibroblasts (ESFs) into decidual stromal cells (DSCs) under the combined action of progesterone, cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), and other unknown maternal signals (Carter and Mess, 2017; Gellersen et al., 2007; Gellersen and Brosens, 2003; Kin et al., 2016; Kin et al., 2015; Mess and Carter, 2006), deeply invasive interstitial hemochorial placentas (Carter et al., 2015; Pijnenborg et al., 2011a; Pijnenborg et al., 2011b; Soares et al., 2018), menstruation (Burley, 1979; Emera et al., 2012b; Finn, 1998; Strassmann, 1996), and a unique but unknown parturition signal (Csapo, 1956; Csapo and Pinto-Dantas, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research on primate reproduction.

claim: Catarrhine primates have evolved deeply invasive interstitial hemochorial placentas.
source: Catarrhine primates, for example, have evolved spontaneous decidualization (differentiation) of endometrial stromal fibroblasts (ESFs) into decidual stromal cells (DSCs) under the combined action of progesterone, cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), and other unknown maternal signals (Carter and Mess, 2017; Gellersen et al., 2007; Gellersen and Brosens, 2003; Kin et al., 2016; Kin et al., 2015; Mess and Carter, 2006), deeply invasive interstitial hemochorial placentas (Carter et al., 2015; Pijnenborg et al., 2011a; Pijnenborg et al., 2011b; Soares et al., 2018), menstruation (Burley, 1979; Emera et al., 2012b; Finn, 1998; Strassmann, 1996), and a unique but unknown parturition signal (Csapo, 1956; Csapo and Pinto-Dantas, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Catarrhine primates have evolved menstruation.
source: Catarrhine primates, for example, have evolved spontaneous decidualization (differentiation) of endometrial stromal fibroblasts (ESFs) into decidual stromal cells (DSCs) under the combined action of progesterone, cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), and other unknown maternal signals (Carter and Mess, 2017; Gellersen et al., 2007; Gellersen and Brosens, 2003; Kin et al., 2016; Kin et al., 2015; Mess and Carter, 2006), deeply invasive interstitial hemochorial placentas (Carter et al., 2015; Pijnenborg et al., 2011a; Pijnenborg et al., 2011b; Soares et al., 2018), menstruation (Burley, 1979; Emera et al., 2012b; Finn, 1998; Strassmann, 1996), and a unique but unknown parturition signal (Csapo, 1956; Csapo and Pinto-Dantas, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Catarrhine primates have a unique but unknown parturition signal.
source: Catarrhine primates, for example, have evolved spontaneous decidualization (differentiation) of endometrial stromal fibroblasts (ESFs) into decidual stromal cells (DSCs) under the combined action of progesterone, cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), and other unknown maternal signals (Carter and Mess, 2017; Gellersen et al., 2007; Gellersen and Brosens, 2003; Kin et al., 2016; Kin et al., 2015; Mess and Carter, 2006), deeply invasive interstitial hemochorial placentas (Carter et al., 2015; Pijnenborg et al., 2011a; Pijnenborg et al., 2011b; Soares et al., 2018), menstruation (Burley, 1979; Emera et al., 2012b; Finn, 1998; Strassmann, 1996), and a unique but unknown parturition signal (Csapo, 1956; Csapo and Pinto-Dantas, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Humans have evolved interstitial trophoblast invasion, in which the blastocyst is embedded and encased entirely within the uterine endometrium.
source: Humans have evolved interstitial trophoblast invasion, in which the blastocyst is embedded and encased entirely within the uterine endometrium (McGowen et al., 2014; Norwitz et al., 2001; Salamonsen, 1999), shorter interbirth intervals (Galdikas and Wood, 1990), and longer pregnancy and labor (Bourne, 1970; Keeling and Roberts, 1972) than other primates.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Humans have shorter interbirth intervals than other primates.
source: Humans have evolved interstitial trophoblast invasion, in which the blastocyst is embedded and encased entirely within the uterine endometrium (McGowen et al., 2014; Norwitz et al., 2001; Salamonsen, 1999), shorter interbirth intervals (Galdikas and Wood, 1990), and longer pregnancy and labor (Bourne, 1970; Keeling and Roberts, 1972) than other primates.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Humans have longer pregnancy and labor than other primates.
source: Humans have evolved interstitial trophoblast invasion, in which the blastocyst is embedded and encased entirely within the uterine endometrium (McGowen et al., 2014; Norwitz et al., 2001; Salamonsen, 1999), shorter interbirth intervals (Galdikas and Wood, 1990), and longer pregnancy and labor (Bourne, 1970; Keeling and Roberts, 1972) than other primates.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Humans are particularly susceptible to pregnancy complications such as preeclampsia and preterm birth compared to other primates.
source: Humans also are particularly susceptible to pregnancy complications such as preeclampsia (Crosley et al., 2013; Elliot, 2017; Marshall et al., 2018), and preterm birth (Phillips et al., 2015; Rokas et al., 2020; Wildman et al., 2011) than other primates.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The complete dataset includes expression information for 21,750 genes and 33 species.
source: The complete dataset includes expression information for 21,750 genes and 33 species, which were collected at different gestational times from early- to midpregnancy, by multiple labs, and sequencing methods.
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: Genes with TPM ≥2.0 were considered expressed (state = 1), genes with TPM <2.0 were considered not expressed (state = 0).
source: Therefore, we transformed quantitative gene expression values coded as transcripts per million (TPM) into discrete character states such that genes with TPM ≥2.0 were considered expressed (state = 1), genes with TPM <2.0 were considered not expressed (state = 0), and missing genes coded as unknown (?; Box 1).
evidence: This describes the methodology for binary encoding of gene expression data.

claim: Multidimensional scaling (MDS) of species based on gene expression levels (TPMs) was essentially random.
source: Consistent with significant noise reduction, multidimensional scaling (MDS) of species based on gene expression levels (TPMs) was essentially random (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), whereas MDS of the binary encoded dataset grouped species by phylogenetic relatedness (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the MDS plot shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MDS of the binary encoded dataset grouped species by phylogenetic relatedness.
source: Consistent with significant noise reduction, multidimensional scaling (MDS) of species based on gene expression levels (TPMs) was essentially random (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), whereas MDS of the binary encoded dataset grouped species by phylogenetic relatedness (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the MDS plot shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Internal branch lengths of the gene expression tree were generally very short while terminal branches were much longer, indicating pronounced species-specific divergence in endometrial gene expression.
source: Internal branch lengths of the gene expression tree were generally very short while terminal branches were much longer, indicating pronounced species-specific divergence in endometrial gene expression (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Human, baboon, Rhesus monkey, and Pig-Tailed macaque formed a distinct group from other Eutherians, indicating that catarrhine primates have an endometrial gene expression profile during pregnancy that is distinct even from other Eutherians.
source: Human, baboon, Rhesus monkey, and Pig-Tailed macaque formed a distinct group from other Eutherians (cluster 5), indicating that catarrhine primates have an endometrial gene expression profile during pregnancy that is distinct even from other Eutherians (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on the MDS clustering shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 923 genes gained endometrial expression in the human lineage with Bayesian posterior probabilities (BPPs) ≥0.80.
source: We identified 923 genes that gained endometrial expression in the human lineage with Bayesian posterior probabilities (BPPs) ≥0.80 (Figure 2—source data 2; Box 2).
evidence: This is based on the ancestral reconstruction analysis.

claim: Genes that gained endometrial expression in the human lineage are enriched in 54 pathways, 102 biological process Gene Ontology (GO) terms, and 91 disease ontologies at a false discovery rate (FDR) ≤0.10.
source: These genes are enriched in 54 pathways, 102 biological process Gene Ontology (GO) terms, and 91 disease ontologies at a false discovery rate (FDR) ≤0.10 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on overrepresentation analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Enriched pathways for genes that gained endometrial expression in the human lineage include 'GPCRs, Class A Rhodopsin-like', 'Signaling by GPCR', 'Cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction', 'Allograft Rejection', and 'Graft-versus-host disease'.
source: Among enriched pathways were 'GPCRs, Class A Rhodopsin-like', 'Signaling by GPCR', 'Cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction', 'Allograft Rejection', and 'Graft-versus-host disease'.
evidence: This is based on pathway enrichment analysis.

claim: The majority of enriched GO terms for genes that gained endometrial expression in the human lineage were related to signaling processes, such as 'cAMP-mediated signaling' and 'serotonin receptor signaling pathway' or to the immune system, such as 'acute inflammatory response' and 'regulation of immune system process'.
source: The majority of enriched GO terms were related to signaling processes, such as 'cAMP-mediated signaling' and 'serotonin receptor signaling pathway' or to the immune system, such as 'acute inflammatory response' and 'regulation of immune system process'.
evidence: This is based on GO term enrichment analysis.

claim: The majority of enriched disease ontologies for genes that gained endometrial expression in the human lineage were related to the immune system and pregnancy complications.
source: The majority of enriched disease ontologies were related to the immune system, such as 'Autoimmune Diseases', 'Immune System Disease', 'Inflammation', 'Asthma', 'Rheumatic Diseases', 'Dermatitis', 'Celiac Diseases', and 'Organ Transplantation', as well as 'Pregnancy', 'Pregnancy, First Trimester', 'Infertility', 'Habitual Abortion', 'Chorioamnionitis', 'Pre-Eclampsia', and 'Preterm Birth', consistent with observations that women with systemic autoimmune diseases have an elevated risk of delivering preterm (Kolstad et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on disease ontology enrichment analysis and supported by a citation.

claim: Women with systemic autoimmune diseases have an elevated risk of delivering preterm.
source: The majority of enriched disease ontologies were related to the immune system, such as 'Autoimmune Diseases', 'Immune System Disease', 'Inflammation', 'Asthma', 'Rheumatic Diseases', 'Dermatitis', 'Celiac Diseases', and 'Organ Transplantation', as well as 'Pregnancy', 'Pregnancy, First Trimester', 'Infertility', 'Habitual Abortion', 'Chorioamnionitis', 'Pre-Eclampsia', and 'Preterm Birth', consistent with observations that women with systemic autoimmune diseases have an elevated risk of delivering preterm (Kolstad et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: 771 genes lost endometrial expression in the human lineage with BPP ≥0.80.
source: Seven hundred and seventy-one genes lost endometrial expression in the lineage with BPP ≥0.80 (Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is based on the ancestral reconstruction analysis.

claim: Genes that lost endometrial expression in the human lineage were enriched in 48 pathways, 42 biological process GO terms, and 3 disease ontologies at FDR ≤0.10.
source: These genes were enriched in 48 pathways, 42 biological process GO terms, and 3 disease ontologies at FDR ≤0.10 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on overrepresentation analysis.

claim: Enriched pathways for genes that lost endometrial expression in the human lineage include 'immune system', 'pregnancy', 'pregnancy first trimester', 'infertility', 'habitual abortion', 'preeclampsia', and 'preterm birth'.
source: Enriched pathways included 'immune system', 'pregnancy', 'pregnancy first trimester', 'infertility', 'habitual abortion', 'preeclampsia', and 'preterm birth'.
evidence: This is based on pathway enrichment analysis.

claim: Genes that lost endometrial expression in the human lineage were enriched in disease ontologies including 'Preterm Birth', 'Selenocysteine Synthesis' and 'Selenoamino Acid Metabolism'.
source: Unlike genes that gained endometrial expression in the human lineage, those that lost endometrial expression were enriched in disease ontologies unrelated to the immune system, but did include 'Preterm Birth', as well as 'Selenocysteine Synthesis' and 'Selenoamino Acid Metabolism', the latter two which have been previously implicated in preterm birth by genome-wide association study (GWAS; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on disease ontology enrichment analysis and supported by a citation.

claim: Selenocysteine Synthesis and Selenoamino Acid Metabolism have been previously implicated in preterm birth by genome-wide association study.
source: Unlike genes that gained endometrial expression in the human lineage, those that lost endometrial expression were enriched in disease ontologies unrelated to the immune system, but did include 'Preterm Birth', as well as 'Selenocysteine Synthesis' and 'Selenoamino Acid Metabolism', the latter two which have been previously implicated in preterm birth by genome-wide association study (GWAS; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a GWAS study.

claim: Genes that gained or lost endometrial expression during pregnancy in the stem lineage of primates did not include terms related to the immune system or pregnancy.
source: In stark contrast, genes that gained (+) or lost (−) endometrial expression during pregnancy in the stem lineage of primates (+63/−34) did not include terms related to the immune system or pregnancy.
evidence: This is based on enrichment analysis of genes that changed expression in the primate stem lineage.

claim: Human recruited genes were enriched in five of six endometrial stromal lineage cells, including perivascular endometrial mesenchymal stem cells (pvEMSCs) and four populations of DSCs, as well as plasmocytes, endothelial cells (ECs), DCs, and extravillus cytotrophoblasts.
source: Remarkably, human recruited genes were enriched in five of six endometrial stromal lineage cells, including perivascular endometrial mesenchymal stem cells (pvEMSCs) and four populations of DSCs, as well as plasmocytes, endothelial cells (ECs), DCs, and extravillus cytotrophoblasts (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on single-cell RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Pseudotime single-cell trajectory analysis of endometrial stromal lineage cells identified six distinct populations corresponding to a perivascular mesenchymal stem cell like endometrial stromal population (pvEMSC) population and five populations of DSCs (DSC1–5).
source: Pseudotime single-cell trajectory analysis of endometrial stromal lineage cells identified six distinct populations corresponding to a perivascular mesenchymal stem cell like endometrial stromal population (pvEMSC) population and five populations of DSCs (DSC1–5), as well as cells between pvEMSCs and DSCs that likely represent nondecidualized ESFs and ESFs that have initiated decidualization (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is based on pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: ESFs that decidualize branch into two distinct lineages, termed lineage 1 DSCs (DSC1–DSC3) and lineage 2 DSCs (DSC4 and DSC5).
source: In addition, ESFs that decidualize branch into two distinct lineages, which we term lineage 1 DSCs (DSC1–DSC3) and lineage 2 DSCs (DSC4 and DSC5) (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is based on pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: HTR2B independently evolved endometrial expression at least seven times, including in the human lineage.
source: To explore the history of HTR2B expression in the endometrium in greater detail, we plotted extant and ancestral gene expression probabilities on tetrapod phylogeny and found that it independently evolved endometrial expression at least seven times, including in the human lineage (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on ancestral reconstruction shown in Figure 5A.

claim: HTR2B expression was almost entirely restricted to the DSC cluster.
source: To investigate which cell types express HTR2B, we used the scRNA-Seq dataset from the first trimester maternal–fetal interface and found that HTR2B expression was almost entirely restricted to the DSC cluster (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on single-cell RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: HTR2B expression is transiently downregulated during the initial inflammatory decidual phase but upregulated upon the emergence of decidual cells and senescence decidual cells after 4 days of differentiation.
source: We further explored the expression dynamics HTR2B during decidualization using a scRNA-Seq time-course dataset (Lucas et al., 2020) and found that its expression is transiently downregulated during the initial inflammatory decidual phase but upregulated upon the emergence of decidual cells and senescence decidual cells after 4 days of differentiation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on time-course scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: HTR2B was the only serotonin receptor expressed in either human ESFs or DSCs at TPM ≥2.
source: HTR2B was also the only serotonin receptor expressed in either human ESFs or DSCs at TPM ≥2 (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) and was highly expressed in uterine tissues (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: HTR2B was highly expressed in uterine tissues.
source: HTR2B was also the only serotonin receptor expressed in either human ESFs or DSCs at TPM ≥2 (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) and was highly expressed in uterine tissues (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on GTEx tissue expression data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: HTR2B was only expressed in human and mouse ESFs, but not in ESFs at TPM ≥2 from other species in a multispecies ESF RNA-Seq dataset.
source: Additionally, we found that HTR2B was only expressed in human and mouse ESFs, but not in ESFs at TPM ≥2 from other species in a previously generated multispecies ESF RNA-Seq dataset (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on multispecies RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: HTR2B is expressed in most lineage 1 DSCs, which coexpress other genes such as IL15, INSR, and PRDM1.
source: Pseudotime single-cell trajectory analysis of endometrial stromal lineage cells indicates that HTR2B is expressed in most lineage 1 DSCs, which coexpress other genes such as IL15, INSR, and PRDM1 (Figure 5D); HTR2B is also expressed by a minority of lineage 2 DSCs, ESFs, and PVCs (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: HTR2B is also expressed by a minority of lineage 2 DSCs, ESFs, and PVCs.
source: Pseudotime single-cell trajectory analysis of endometrial stromal lineage cells indicates that HTR2B is expressed in most lineage 1 DSCs, which coexpress other genes such as IL15, INSR, and PRDM1 (Figure 5D); HTR2B is also expressed by a minority of lineage 2 DSCs, ESFs, and PVCs (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: 194 genes were differentially expressed between HTR2B+ and HTR2B− DSCs.
source: One hundred and ninety-four genes were differentially expressed between HTR2B+ and HTR2B− DSCs (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Genes differentially expressed between HTR2B+ and HTR2B− DSCs were enriched in numerous pathways including 'Regulation of Insulin-like Growth Factor (IGF) transport and uptake by Insulin-like Growth Factor Binding Proteins (IGFBPs)', 'Complement and coagulation cascades', 'BMP2–WNT4–FOXO1 Pathway in Human Primary Endometrial Stromal Cell Differentiation', 'IL-18 signaling pathway', and disease ontologies including 'Small-for-dates baby', 'Premature Birth', 'Inflammation', 'Fetal Growth Retardation', 'Pregnancy Complications', 'Hematologic Complications', and 'Spontaneous abortion'.
source: These genes were enriched in numerous pathways including 'Regulation of Insulin-like Growth Factor (IGF) transport and uptake by Insulin-like Growth Factor Binding Proteins (IGFBPs)', 'Complement and coagulation cascades', 'BMP2–WNT4–FOXO1 Pathway in Human Primary Endometrial Stromal Cell Differentiation', 'IL-18 signaling pathway', and disease ontologies including 'Small-for-dates baby', 'Premature Birth', 'Inflammation', 'Fetal Growth Retardation', 'Pregnancy Complications', 'Hematologic Complications', and 'Spontaneous abortion' (Figure 5F and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: HTR2B was highly expressed in ESFs and downregulated during differentiation (decidualization) by cAMP/progesterone into DSCs.
source: To determine if HTR2B expression was regulated by progesterone, we used previously published RNA-Seq data from human ESFs and ESFs differentiated into DSCs with cAMP/progesterone (Mazur et al., 2015). HTR2B was highly expressed in ESFs and downregulated during differentiation (decidualization) by cAMP/progesterone into DSCs (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: HTR2B has hallmarks of an expressed gene in DSCs, including residing in a region open chromatin, an H3K4me3 and H3K27ac marked promoter and polymerase II binding.
source: HTR2B has hallmarks of an expressed gene in DSCs, including residing in a region open chromatin assessed by previously published FAIRE-Seq data (Figure 6B), an H3K4me3 and H3K27ac marked promoter and polymerase II binding, as well as a promoter that makes long-range loops to binding sites for transcription factors that orchestrate decidualization such as the progesterone receptor A isoform (PGR-A), FOXO1, FOSL2, GATA2, and NR2F2 (COUP-TFII) in previously published ChIP-Seq data (see methods) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-Seq and FAIRE-Seq data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The HTR2B promoter makes long-range loops to binding sites for transcription factors that orchestrate decidualization such as PGR-A, FOXO1, FOSL2, GATA2, and NR2F2 (COUP-TFII).
source: HTR2B has hallmarks of an expressed gene in DSCs, including residing in a region open chromatin assessed by previously published FAIRE-Seq data (Figure 6B), an H3K4me3 and H3K27ac marked promoter and polymerase II binding, as well as a promoter that makes long-range loops to binding sites for transcription factors that orchestrate decidualization such as the progesterone receptor A isoform (PGR-A), FOXO1, FOSL2, GATA2, and NR2F2 (COUP-TFII) in previously published ChIP-Seq data (see methods) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-Seq and HiChIP data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The HTR2B promoter makes several long-range interactions to transcription factor-bound sites as assessed by H3K27ac HiChIP data.
source: The HTR2B promoter also makes several long-range interactions to transcription factor-bound sites as assessed by H3K27ac HiChIP data generated from a normal hTERT-immortalized endometrial cell line (E6E7hTERT; see methods) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on HiChIP data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Knockdown of PGR, FOXO1, and GATA2 upregulated HTR2B in DSCs.
source: Consistent with regulation by these transcription factors, knockdown of PGR, FOXO1, and GATA2 upregulated HTR2B in DSCs (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: HTR2B is differentially regulated throughout menstrual cycle and pregnancy.
source: HTR2B is also differentially regulated throughout menstrual cycle (Figure 6D) and pregnancy (Figure 6E), and is expressed in DSCs in the endometrium during the window of implantation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on gene expression data shown in Figure 6D and 6E.

claim: HTR2B is expressed in DSCs in the endometrium during the window of implantation.
source: HTR2B is also differentially regulated throughout menstrual cycle (Figure 6D) and pregnancy (Figure 6E), and is expressed in DSCs in the endometrium during the window of implantation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescent staining shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The serum response element (SRE) reporter in DSCs was responsive to 1000 μM serotonin treatment.
source: Two pathway reporters were responsive to serotonin: (1) the serum response element (SRE) reporter in DSCs treated with 1000 μM serotonin (unpaired mean difference between is 1.35 [95.0% CI 0.624, 2.69], two-sided permutation t-test p = 0.00); and (2) the cAMP/PKA response element (CRE) reporter in ESFs treated with 1000 μM serotonin (unpaired mean difference between is 0.296 [95.0% CI 0.161, 0.43], two-sided permutation t-test p = 0.00) and in DSCs treated with 50 μM (unpaired mean difference = −10.1 [95% CI −13.8, −6.28], two-sided permutation t-test p = 0.001), 200 μM (unpaired mean difference = 17.4 [95% CI 11.6, 24.6], two-sided permutation t-test p = 0.0004), and 1000 μM serotonin (unpaired mean difference is 16.7 [95 %CI 7.67, 26.8], two-sided permutation t-test p = 0.006) (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The cAMP/PKA response element (CRE) reporter in ESFs was responsive to 1000 μM serotonin treatment.
source: Two pathway reporters were responsive to serotonin: (1) the serum response element (SRE) reporter in DSCs treated with 1000 μM serotonin (unpaired mean difference between is 1.35 [95.0% CI 0.624, 2.69], two-sided permutation t-test p = 0.00); and (2) the cAMP/PKA response element (CRE) reporter in ESFs treated with 1000 μM serotonin (unpaired mean difference between is 0.296 [95.0% CI 0.161, 0.43], two-sided permutation t-test p = 0.00) and in DSCs treated with 50 μM (unpaired mean difference = −10.1 [95% CI −13.8, −6.28], two-sided permutation t-test p = 0.001), 200 μM (unpaired mean difference = 17.4 [95% CI 11.6, 24.6], two-sided permutation t-test p = 0.0004), and 1000 μM serotonin (unpaired mean difference is 16.7 [95 %CI 7.67, 26.8], two-sided permutation t-test p = 0.006) (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The cAMP/PKA response element (CRE) reporter in DSCs was responsive to 50 μM, 200 μM, and 1000 μM serotonin treatment.
source: Two pathway reporters were responsive to serotonin: (1) the serum response element (SRE) reporter in DSCs treated with 1000 μM serotonin (unpaired mean difference between is 1.35 [95.0% CI 0.624, 2.69], two-sided permutation t-test p = 0.00); and (2) the cAMP/PKA response element (CRE) reporter in ESFs treated with 1000 μM serotonin (unpaired mean difference between is 0.296 [95.0% CI 0.161, 0.43], two-sided permutation t-test p = 0.00) and in DSCs treated with 50 μM (unpaired mean difference = −10.1 [95% CI −13.8, −6.28], two-sided permutation t-test p = 0.001), 200 μM (unpaired mean difference = 17.4 [95% CI 11.6, 24.6], two-sided permutation t-test p = 0.0004), and 1000 μM serotonin (unpaired mean difference is 16.7 [95 %CI 7.67, 26.8], two-sided permutation t-test p = 0.006) (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: PDCD1LG2 was expressed by several cell types at the first trimester maternal–fetal interface, including DCs, macrophages, ESFs and DSCs, and multiple trophoblast lineages.
source: We found that PDCD1LG2 was expressed by several cell types at the first trimester maternal–fetal interface, including DCs, macrophages, ESFs and DSCs, and multiple trophoblast lineages (Figure 7B), and is highly expressed in uterine tissues (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on single-cell RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: PDCD1LG2 is highly expressed in uterine tissues.
source: We found that PDCD1LG2 was expressed by several cell types at the first trimester maternal–fetal interface, including DCs, macrophages, ESFs and DSCs, and multiple trophoblast lineages (Figure 7B), and is highly expressed in uterine tissues (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on GTEx tissue expression data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only 3%–5% of DSCs, 3% of DCs, 14% of macrophage, and 66% of cytotrophoblasts express PDCD1LG2.
source: While each of these cell-type populations has individual cells with high-level PDCD1LG2 expression, only 3%–5% of DSCs, 3 % of DCs, 14 % of macrophage, and 66 % of cytotrophoblasts express PDCD1LG2 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on single-cell RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: PDCD1LG2 was highly expressed in human but either moderately or not expressed in ESFs from other species.
source: Consistent with recent recruitment in the human lineage, PDCD1LG2 was highly expressed in human but either moderately or not expressed in ESFs from other species (Figure 7D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on multispecies RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The human PDCD1LG2 locus has the hallmarks of an actively expressed gene, such as a promoter marked by H3K27ac, H3K4me3, and H3K4me1, and binding sites for several transcription factors.
source: The human PDCD1LG2 locus has the hallmarks of an actively expressed gene, such as a promoter marked by H3K27ac, H3K4me3, and H3K4me1, and binding sites for several transcription factors in previously published ChIP-Seq data from DSCs (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The PDCD1LG2 promoter makes several long-range interactions to transcription factor-bound sites, including downstream site that is in the region of open chromatin and bound by PGR/GATA/FOXO1.
source: The PDCD1LG2 promoter also makes several long-range interactions to transcription factor-bound sites, including downstream site that is in the region of open chromatin and bound by PGR/GATA/FOXO1 (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is based on HiChIP and ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: PDCD1LG2 was highly expressed in ESFs and DSCs but downregulated by cAMP/progesterone treatment.
source: PDCD1LG2 was highly expressed in ESFs and DSCs (Figure 7F) but downregulated by cAMP/progesterone treatment (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 7F and 7G.

claim: Knockdown of PGR upregulated PDCD1LG2 in DSCs.
source: Knockdown of PGR and FOXO1 up- and downregulated PDCD1LG2 in DSCs, respectively (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is based on siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Knockdown of FOXO1 downregulated PDCD1LG2 in DSCs.
source: Knockdown of PGR and FOXO1 up- and downregulated PDCD1LG2 in DSCs, respectively (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is based on siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 7G.

claim: PDCD1LG2 introns contain several single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) previously associated with gestational duration and number of lifetime pregnancies as assessed by GWAS.
source: PDCD1LG2 introns also contain several single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) previously associated with gestational duration and number of lifetime pregnancies as assessed by GWAS (Aschebrook-Kilfoy et al., 2015; Sakabe et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2017), albeit with marginal p values, implicating PDCD1LG2 in regulating gestation length (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is based on GWAS data shown in Figure 7E and supported by citations.

claim: CORIN is a serine protease which promotes uterine spiral artery remodeling and trophoblast invasion.
source: Among the human recruited genes enriched in disease ontologies related to preeclampsia (Figure 2) is CORIN (Figure 8A), a serine protease which promotes uterine spiral artery remodeling and trophoblast invasion (Cui et al., 2012; Yan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CORIN was exclusively expressed by a subset of endometrial stromal lineage cells.
source: We found that CORIN was exclusively expressed by a subset of endometrial stromal lineage cells (Figure 8B and C), dramatically upregulated in DSCs by cAMP/progesterone treatment (Figure 8D), and highly expressed in uterine tissues (Figure 8—figure supplement 1; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on single-cell RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: CORIN was dramatically upregulated in DSCs by cAMP/progesterone treatment.
source: We found that CORIN was exclusively expressed by a subset of endometrial stromal lineage cells (Figure 8B and C), dramatically upregulated in DSCs by cAMP/progesterone treatment (Figure 8D), and highly expressed in uterine tissues (Figure 8—figure supplement 1; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: CORIN is highly expressed in uterine tissues.
source: We found that CORIN was exclusively expressed by a subset of endometrial stromal lineage cells (Figure 8B and C), dramatically upregulated in DSCs by cAMP/progesterone treatment (Figure 8D), and highly expressed in uterine tissues (Figure 8—figure supplement 1; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on GTEx tissue expression data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The CORIN locus has hallmarks of an actively expressed gene in DSCs, including a promoter in a region of open chromatin and marked by H3K4me3.
source: The CORIN locus has hallmarks of an actively expressed gene in DSCs, including a promoter in a region of open chromatin assessed by previously published ATAC- and DNase-Seq data and marked by H3K4me3 in previously published ChIP-Seq data (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is based on ATAC-Seq, DNase-Seq, and ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The CORIN promoter makes long-range interactions to transcription factor-bound sites as assessed by HiChIP, including an upstream site bound by PGR, FOSL2, GATA2, FOXO1, and NR2F2.
source: The CORIN promoter also makes long-range interactions to transcription factor-bound sites as assessed by HiChIP, including an upstream site bound by PGR, FOSL2, GATA2, FOXO1, and NR2F2 in previously published ChIP-Seq data from DSCs (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is based on HiChIP and ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Knockdown of PGR, NR2F2, and GATA2 downregulated CORIN expression in DSCs.
source: Consistent with these observations, knockdown of PGR, NR2F2, and GATA2 downregulated CORIN expression in DSCs (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is based on siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Remodeling of the transcriptome and functions of the endometrial stromal cell lineage has played a particularly important role in the evolution of human-specific pregnancy traits.
source: These data suggest that remodeling of the transcriptome and functions of the endometrial stromal cell lineage has played a particularly important role in the evolution of human-specific pregnancy traits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enrichment of human recruited genes in endometrial stromal lineage cells.

claim: Decidual stromal cells evolved in the stem lineage of Eutherian mammals.
source: It is also interesting to note that DSCs evolved in the stem lineage of Eutherian mammals (Carter and Mess, 2017; Gellersen et al., 2007; Gellersen and Brosens, 2003; Kin et al., 2016; Kin et al., 2015; Mess and Carter, 2006), coincident with a wave of gene expression recruitments and losses that also dramatically remodeled their transcriptomes (Kin et al., 2015; Lynch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The endometrial stromal cell lineage has repeatedly been the target of evolutionary changes related to pregnancy.
source: Thus, the endometrial stromal cell lineage has repeatedly been the target of evolutionary changes related to pregnancy, highlighting the importance of DSCs in the origins and divergence of pregnancy traits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the evolutionary history of DSCs and gene expression changes.

claim: Endometrial stromal lineage cells may play a dominant role in the ontogenesis of adverse pregnancy outcomes.
source: These data also suggest that endometrial stromal lineage cells may play a dominant role in the ontogenesis of adverse pregnancy outcomes.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the enrichment of human recruited genes in these cells and their association with adverse pregnancy outcomes.

claim: Serotonin treatment affected RAS/MAPK(ERK) and cAMP/PKA signaling pathways, which are essential for decidualization.
source: Though a role for serotonin in the endometrium has not previously been reported, we found that serotonin treatment effected RAS/MAPK(ERK) and cAMP/PKA signaling pathways, which are essential for decidualization, and that HTR2B is dynamically expressed during menstrual cycle and pregnancy, reaching a low at term.
evidence: This is based on the luciferase reporter assays showing pathway activation.

claim: The human placenta is a source of serotonin throughout gestation.
source: Previous studies have shown that the human placenta is a source of serotonin throughout gestation (Clark et al., 1980; Kliman et al., 2018; Laurent et al., 2017; Ranzil et al., 2019; Rosenfeld, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Levels of both serotonin (5-HT) and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), the main metabolite of serotonin, are highest in amniotic fluid near term and during labor.
source: For example, levels of both serotonin (5-HT) and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), the main metabolite of serotonin, are highest in amniotic fluid near term and during labor (Jones and Pycock, 1978; Koren et al., 1961; Loose and Paterson, 1966; Tu and Wong, 1976) while placental monoamine oxidase activity (which metabolizes serotonin) is lowest at term (Koren et al., 1965).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Placental monoamine oxidase activity (which metabolizes serotonin) is lowest at term.
source: For example, levels of both serotonin (5-HT) and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), the main metabolite of serotonin, are highest in amniotic fluid near term and during labor (Jones and Pycock, 1978; Koren et al., 1961; Loose and Paterson, 1966; Tu and Wong, 1976) while placental monoamine oxidase activity (which metabolizes serotonin) is lowest at term (Koren et al., 1965).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A single dose of the monoamine oxidase inhibitor paraglyline hydrochloride can induce abortion in humans and other animals.
source: Furthermore, a single dose of the monoamine oxidase inhibitor paraglyline hydrochloride can induce abortion in humans and other animals (Koren et al., 1966)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors is associated with preterm birth.
source: Consistent with a potential role in regulating gestation length and parturition, use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors is associated with preterm birth (Eke et al., 2016; Grzeskowiak et al., 2012; Huybrechts et al., 2014; Ross et al., 2013; Sujan et al., 2017; Yonkers et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: 5-HIAA inhibits RAS/MAPK signaling, potentially by competing with serotonin for binding sites on serotonin receptors.
source: 5-HIAA also inhibits RAS/MAPK signaling, potentially by competing with serotonin for binding sites on serotonin receptors (Chen et al., 2011; Klein et al., 2018; Schmid et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: PD-1 is a member of the immunoglobulin superfamily expressed on T cells and pro-B cells that regulates a critical immune checkpoint.
source: PD-1, a member of the immunoglobulin superfamily expressed on T cells and pro-B cells, regulates a critical immune checkpoint that plays an essential role in downregulating immune responses and promoting self-tolerance by suppressing T-cell inflammatory activity (Patsoukis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research and represents established knowledge.

claim: PD-1 has two ligands, CD274 (PD-L1) and PDCD1LG2 (PD-L2), which upon binding PD-1 promote apoptosis in antigen-specific T cells and inhibit apoptosis in anti-inflammatory Tregs.
source: PD-1 has two ligands, CD274 (PD-L1) and PDCD1LG2 (PD-L2), which upon binding PD-1 promote apoptosis in antigen-specific T cells and inhibit apoptosis in anti-inflammatory Tregs (Patsoukis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research and represents established knowledge.

claim: PDCD1LG2 expression is generally restricted to professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs) such as DCs and macrophages.
source: Unlike CD274, which is constitutively expressed at low levels in numerous cell types and induced by IFN-gamma, PDCD1LG2 expression is generally restricted to professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs) such as DCs and macrophages and has a fourfold stronger affinity for PD-1 than does CD274 (Ghiotto et al., 2010; Latchman et al., 2001; Sharpe et al., 2007; Sharpe and Pauken, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: PDCD1LG2 has a fourfold stronger affinity for PD-1 than does CD274.
source: Unlike CD274, which is constitutively expressed at low levels in numerous cell types and induced by IFN-gamma, PDCD1LG2 expression is generally restricted to professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs) such as DCs and macrophages and has a fourfold stronger affinity for PD-1 than does CD274 (Ghiotto et al., 2010; Latchman et al., 2001; Sharpe et al., 2007; Sharpe and Pauken, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The higher affinity of PDCD1LG2 for PD-1 emerged in the Eutherian stem lineage.
source: Remarkably, this higher affinity emerged in the Eutherian stem lineage (Philips et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A subpopulation of human DSCs have co-opted some of the immune regulatory functions of professional APCs.
source: These data suggest that a subpopulation of human DSCs have co-opted some of the immune regulatory functions of professional APCs, which may have been significantly augmented in the human lineage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression of PDCD1LG2 in DSCs and its known immune regulatory function.

claim: CORIN-mediated ANP production in the uterus during pregnancy has been shown to promote spiral artery remodeling and trophoblast invasion.
source: CORIN, which converts pro-atrial natriuretic peptide (pro-ANP) to biologically active ANP (Yan et al., 2000). CORIN-mediated ANP production in the uterus during pregnancy has been shown to promote spiral artery remodeling and trophoblast invasion (Cui et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Co-option of CORIN into endometrial expression may have contributed to the evolution of particularly deep trophoblast invasion and extensive spiral artery remodeling in humans and other great apes.
source: These data implicate co-option of CORIN into endometrial expression may have contributed to the evolution of particularly deep trophoblast invasion and extensive spiral artery remodeling in humans and other great apes (Carter et al., 2015; Pijnenborg et al., 2011a; Pijnenborg et al., 2011b; Soares et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on CORIN's function and its recruitment in the human lineage, supported by citations.

claim: CORIN expression is significantly lower in patients with preeclampsia than in normal pregnancies.
source: CORIN expression is also significantly lower in patients with preeclampsia than in normal pregnancies (Cui et al., 2012), suggesting that the co-option of CORIN into human endometrium may predispose humans to preeclampsia.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The co-option of CORIN into human endometrium may predispose humans to preeclampsia.
source: CORIN expression is also significantly lower in patients with preeclampsia than in normal pregnancies (Cui et al., 2012), suggesting that the co-option of CORIN into human endometrium may predispose humans to preeclampsia.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on CORIN's expression pattern and association with preeclampsia.
